nameStory: The Carolina Sphinx gets its name from its discovery and prevalence in the Carolinas, though it ranges throughout much of the Americas. The 'sphinx' part comes from the caterpillar's habit of rearing up its front end when threatened, resembling the ancient Egyptian sphinx statue in its upright, alert posture.
description: The Carolina Sphinx is a large, powerful moth that's active at dusk and night, often mistaken for a small hummingbird as it hovers at flowers. Adults have thick, streamlined bodies and long, narrow wings that can span up to 5 inches across. The moth is grayish-brown with intricate patterns, while its famous caterpillar stage - the tobacco hornworm - is a bright green giant that can grow as thick as your thumb and nearly 4 inches long. That distinctive horn on the caterpillar's rear end gives it the 'hornworm' nickname, though it's completely harmless.

idTips.label: Caterpillar Horn Color
idTips.description: The larval stage has a bright red or orange horn protruding from its rear end - this red horn is the key difference from its cousin, the tomato hornworm, which has a dark blue or black horn

idTips.label: White Stripe Pattern
idTips.description: Tobacco hornworm caterpillars have seven diagonal white stripes bordered in black along their sides - these look like straight cigarette lines, unlike the V-shaped markings of tomato hornworms

idTips.label: Adult Flight Pattern
idTips.description: The moth hovers at flowers like a hummingbird, creating an audible humming sound with its rapidly beating wings - you'll hear the buzz before you see the large, gray-brown body

idTips.label: Caterpillar Size and Texture
idTips.description: The green caterpillar feels surprisingly firm and smooth to the touch, not squishy like many caterpillars, and can grow impressively large - often longer than your index finger

idTips.label: Defensive Posture
idTips.description: When disturbed, the caterpillar rears up its front end in a sphinx-like pose, curling into an S-shape that makes it look like it's ready to strike (though it's harmless)

idTips.label: Plant Association
idTips.description: Most often found on plants in the nightshade family - tomatoes, peppers, tobacco, and petunias - where the large caterpillars can quickly defoliate plants

habitat: Carolina Sphinx moths thrive in gardens, farms, and edge habitats throughout New England's warmer areas, particularly where nightshade family plants grow. You'll find the caterpillars munching on tomato plants in vegetable gardens, tobacco fields, and wild nightshades along field edges and disturbed soils. Adults visit flower gardens at dusk, especially favoring deep-throated flowers like petunias, four o'clocks, and tobacco blossoms.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with mating and egg-laying occurring on host plants. Look for tiny, pale green eggs on the undersides of tomato and pepper leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak caterpillar activity occurs through summer months when the large, green hornworms are most visible on garden plants. Adults are active at dusk visiting flowers.
seasonality.fall: Second generation caterpillars mature and pupate in the soil before frost. Some adults may still be seen at flowers on warm evenings in early fall.
seasonality.winter: The species overwinters as brown pupae buried 3-4 inches deep in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger emergence.

funFact: Tobacco hornworms are living chemical warfare specialists - they can actually absorb nicotine from tobacco plants and concentrate it in their bodies as a defense against predators, making themselves toxic to birds and other animals that try to eat them.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the tomato hornworm, but remember: tobacco hornworms have red horns and straight white lines like cigarettes, while tomato hornworms have dark horns and V-shaped white markings like 'vine-ripened' tomatoes. The adults are nearly impossible to distinguish without close examination.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'tobacco' hornworm, this species happily feeds on many plants in the nightshade family, including tomatoes, peppers, and petunias - not just tobacco. The name simply reflects where it was first commonly noticed and studied by farmers.
compareHints: While there are no other Manduca species commonly found in New England, the Carolina Sphinx is most often confused with the closely related tomato hornworm (Manduca quinquemaculata). The two species are so similar that even experts focus on the larval stage differences - red vs. dark horns and straight vs. V-shaped white markings - to tell them apart. Both create the same hovering, hummingbird-like adult moths that visit flowers at dusk.
